items.title: Wendell Brunious interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: We just buried an old guy from the Preservation Hall, Mr. Percy Humphrey.

ctx.x: In other words, continuity and change have to be balanced.

Yes. They have to be. That’s a great way of putting that. They have to be balanced. And if they’re not balanced, we’re going to destroy that tradition, which is in a big threat now. We just buried an old guy from the Preservation Hall, Mr. Percy Humphrey. And you know we tried to keep it as a traditional jazz funeral. But it was, a lot of people started coming in there, some lady playing the flute with tights and you know, a leotard and all this kind of crazy stuff you know. I mean she’s got a right to express…

This makes a case for jazz education going beyond the classroom, into what we call etiquette. Concert etiquette. But I want to say this about yourself, and then talk a little bit. I see you as being an important person, being a relatively young man, from New Orleans, restoring some of the respect of the music and the tradition. Do you see — where do you see yourself?
